---
title: "Frequentist vs Bayesian: Interpreting Intervals"
---

::: {.callout-note title="The platform problem"}
Your scorecard reports an interval, and a stakeholder reads it as "there's a 95%
chance the true effect is in here." That reading is *wrong* for a frequentist
confidence interval and *right* for a Bayesian credible interval. The gap is not
pedantry — it changes how you communicate results, what decision rules are
legitimate, and how you may stop an experiment. This chapter draws the line.
:::

## Two intervals that look identical and mean different things

- **Confidence interval (frequentist).** A statement about the *procedure*: across
  many repetitions, 95% of the intervals it generates cover the true value. It
  says nothing about the probability that *this* interval contains $\theta$ — once
  computed, the interval either covers $\theta$ or it doesn't.
- **Credible interval (Bayesian).** A statement about *this* interval given a
  prior: the posterior probability that $\theta$ lies inside is 95%. It is the
  thing people *think* a CI is — at the cost of requiring a prior.

The widespread misreading of CIs is well documented (Morey et al., *The fallacy
of placing confidence in confidence intervals*). Naming it is part of building a
trustworthy scorecard.

## The same data, both ways

```{python}
# Worked contrast on one dataset:
#   frequentist 95% CI  (e.g. mean ± 1.96·SE)
#   Bayesian 95% credible interval (conjugate or sampled posterior)
# Show numerically how/whether they coincide, and how the credible interval
# shifts as the prior changes — the frequentist interval does not.
```

With a flat/weak prior and a large sample the two often nearly coincide, which is
why the misinterpretation usually "works" — and why it quietly fails with small
samples or informative priors.

## Why it matters for experimentation

- **Decisions.** Bayesian decision rules speak the language of business directly:
  $P(B > A)$, expected loss, expected uplift — see the applied treatment in
  Part IV (Bayesian A/B).
- **Stopping & peeking.** Bayesian methods are *not* automatically immune to the
  peeking problem (Deng et al.); naive optional stopping can still inflate error.
  The rigorous always-valid tools — frequentist confidence sequences and e-values
  — live in Part IV. This chapter only frames the debate; that part resolves it.
- **Communication.** If you want to *say* "95% chance the effect is positive," you
  owe your audience a credible interval and an explicit prior — not a relabeled CI.

## When to use which

A short, honest guide: frequentist CIs as the platform default (no prior to argue
about, well-understood guarantees); Bayesian credible intervals when you have a
defensible prior, want direct probability statements for decisions, or are pooling
across many segments (hierarchical shrinkage, Part VI/Part IV).

## Validate against ground truth (Vega)

```{python}
# The cleanest demonstration of the difference:
#   simulate many experiments with a KNOWN θ.
#   - frequentist 95% CI: coverage should be ≈ 0.95 regardless of θ.
#   - Bayesian 95% credible interval: coverage depends on whether the prior
#     matches the θ-generating process — well-calibrated under a matched prior,
#     biased under a mismatched one.
# Seeing coverage move with the prior makes the interpretation gap concrete.
```
